limitations: The experimental situation (laboratory, short duration, awareness of leaving) limits the generality of findings to macro crowding phenomena in urban environments.
The potency of the room size manipulation may have 'swamped out' the effect of a competitive task set on the perception of crowding within the small room.

Subjects' physical discomfort (small room perceived as more uncomfortable, hotter, and stuffier) may partially explain the lack of a significant room size-x-task set interaction on perceived crowding.
It is impossible to ascertain whether laughter served as a coping response to felt crowding, a pure indication of good humor, or if perceived crowding actually decreased over time.
It is impossible to ascertain whether increased laughter and noise reflected the absence of crowding, a mode of coping, or a nonspatial source of heightened crowding (overstimulation).
Experimenter effects on perceived quietness, name recall, and number of jokes were found but are not uniquely relevant for understanding crowding nor easily interpretable.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated physical, social, and personal determinants of crowding perception in a laboratory setting. It found that smaller room size significantly increased perceived crowding, restriction, and confinement, and decreased patience. A cooperative task set generally reduced perceived crowding, anxiety, and increased game enjoyment, though it paradoxically increased perceived room confinement and attributed aggressiveness to others. Sex of subject moderated several effects: males perceived themselves more aggressive in small rooms, while females felt more aggressive in large rooms. Females generally perceived rooms as quieter and recalled more names than males. The study highlights that crowding is an experiential state influenced by interactions between spatial, social, and personal factors, rather than just density. Limitations include the artificiality of the lab setting and challenges in interpreting behavioral responses like laughter as coping mechanisms versus other social cues.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Increased environmental load (e.g., high density, small space) leads to physiological arousal, which is then interpreted as perceived crowding.

mechanism_chain.description: Physical constraints like small room size increase social density, which can induce physiological arousal and a sense of restrictedness, leading to the perception of crowding.

instruments_used.name: Perceived Crowding Scale
instruments_used.description: Self-report scale using semantic differential items (e.g., restricted-unrestricted, crowded-uncrowded, confined-unconfined).
